mainTopic: שאלה בבעלים: why the time of borrowing decides the exemption, what counts as borrowing, and who counts as 'the owner' (partners, husband, agent, slave)
overview: The גמרא continues discussing שאלה בבעלים, where a borrower is exempt because the owner was working for him. רבא follows רבי יונתן and brings a ברייתא that seems to set two פסוקים against each other. It settles the clash this way: the owner's presence at the time of borrowing is enough, but presence only when the animal is injured or dies is not. After some back-and-forth, the גמרא explains why borrowing is the key moment: from then on the borrower must feed the animal. רב אשי proves the same rule from the words 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ'. רמי בר חמא then asks a series of questions about what counts as borrowing: a sinful use, borrowing just to show off, use worth less than a פרוטה, and two cows worth a פרוטה together. Next come questions about who counts as 'the owner': partners, a husband and wife, an agent, and a slave. The husband and agent questions are tied to older disputes about קנין פירות and שליחות. רבא rules that a slave counts as his master. The amud ends as רמי בר חמא begins a new question about a husband and his wife's property, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבא follows רבי יונתן: the first verse exempts even when the owner was there only once
steps.stepSummary: רבא holds like רבי יונתן and brings a ברייתא. It reads 'If its owner is with him, he shall not pay' as covering both full presence and presence at only one of the two times, and in both cases the borrower is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא agrees with רבי יונתן and explains the פסוקים his way, as a ברייתא teaches: 'If its owner is with him, he shall not pay.' This means when the owner was with him at both times, and it also means when he was with him at one time but not the other. In both cases the borrower is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבא's view and starts a ברייתא that reads the first פסוק broadly: the owner's presence at even one of the two times exempts the borrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two key moments: when the animal was borrowed, and when it was injured or died. Because רבי יונתן lets a phrase apply even to part of what it describes, 'the owner is with him' can mean with him at both times or at just one. Read alone, this פסוק gives an exemption even with partial presence.

keyTerms.meaning: borrowing an animal while its owner is also working for the borrower
it implies / it can be read as meaning

steps.confusionAlert: 'With him' does not mean just standing nearby. It means the owner was working for the borrower. The question is at which moment that has to be true: when the animal was borrowed, or when it was hurt or died.

phrases.english: Rava holds in accordance with Rabbi Yonatan
phrases.notes: רבי יונתן reads a pair like 'his father and his mother' as applying even when only one of them is involved.

phrases.english: and he explains the verses in accordance with Rabbi Yonatan,
as it is taught in a baraita:
"If its owner is with him, he shall not pay."
This implies that he was there at both times,
phrases.notes: 'Both' means both moments: when the animal was borrowed, and when it was injured or died.

phrases.english: and it also implies that when he was there at one time
and not there at the other, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא סָבַר לַהּ כְּרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens רבא's approach as a contrast to the view discussed just before this point.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Read alone, 'If its owner is with him' exempts the borrower even if the owner was present at only one of the two times.

steps.title: The second verse seems to make him liable when the owner was there only once
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא points to the other פסוק, 'If its owner is not with him, he shall surely pay.' Read the same broad way, it makes the borrower חייב when the owner was absent at even one of the times, which clashes with step 1.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is also written: 'If its owner is not with him, he shall surely pay.' This means when the owner was absent at both times, and it also means when he was there at one time but not the other. In both cases the borrower is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises a contradiction: the second פסוק, read the same broad way, makes the borrower pay in the exact mixed case where the first פסוק exempted him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Using רבי יונתן's reading on the second פסוק, 'not with him' can mean not with him at even one of the times. So the mixed case (present once, absent once) is exempt under the first פסוק but liable under the second. The ברייתא now has to explain how both can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: and it is written (bringing another פסוק)
he is not there / was not present

phrases.english: But it is written:
"If its owner is not with him, he shall surely pay";
this implies that he was not there at both times,
and it also implies that when he was there at one time
and not there at the other, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְתִיב: ״בְּעָלָיו אֵין עִמּוֹ שַׁלֵּם יְשַׁלֵּם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets the second פסוק against the reading of the first פסוק in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion of step 1 that the mixed case is exempt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same broad reading applied to the second פסוק makes the very same mixed case liable, so the two פסוקים contradict each other.

steps.title: Resolution: presence at the time of borrowing is what counts
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא resolves the clash by splitting the mixed case. If the owner was there at the time of borrowing, that alone exempts the borrower. If he was there only at the time of injury or death, the borrower is still liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: This comes to tell you: if the owner was with him when the animal was borrowed, he does not need to be with him when it is injured or dies. But if he was with him when it was injured or died, he still needs to have been with him when it was borrowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives each פסוק its own half of the mixed case: presence at the time of borrowing exempts, and presence only at the time of injury or death does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mixed case is really two different cases. The first פסוק ('with him, no pay') covers the case of presence at borrowing only. The second פסוק ('not with him, pay') covers the case of presence at injury or death only. This way neither פסוק is cancelled.

keyTerms.meaning: to tell you (introduces the lesson that settles the problem)
injured and died (the moment of loss)

steps.whatToRemember: According to this ברייתא, as רבא reads it, what counts is whether the owner was with the borrower at the time of שאלה. If he was, the borrower is פטור even if the owner was gone when the animal broke or died. If the owner was there only at the time of loss, the borrower is חייב.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule for שאלה בבעלים in רבא's approach: the time of borrowing decides it.

phrases.english: This comes to tell you:
if he was with him at the time of borrowing,
he does not need to be with him
at the time it is injured or dies;
if he was with him at the time it is injured or dies,
he still needs to have been with him at the time of borrowing.

steps.triggerLanguage: לוֹמַר לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the case: each פסוק applies to a different version of the mixed case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two פסוקים seemed to give opposite rulings for the same mixed case.
steps.terutzMaskana: Presence at borrowing alone exempts; presence at injury or death alone does not.

steps.title: Why not reverse it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the resolution: why not say the opposite, that presence at the time of injury or death is what exempts?
steps.simpleTranslation: I could reverse it! Maybe presence at the time of injury or death is enough, and presence at borrowing is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges step 3 by asking why the split could not go the other way around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both פסוקים fit just as well if we swap which moment matters. So the split in step 3 needs a reason for choosing the time of borrowing over the time of loss.

keyTerms.meaning: I could reverse it (a challenge suggesting the opposite reading)

phrases.english: I could reverse it!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיפוֹךְ אֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the direction of the split given in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The choice of the time of borrowing as the deciding moment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוקים themselves do not say which moment counts, so the opposite split seems just as possible.

steps.title: Borrowing is weightier because it brings the animal into the borrower's domain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that it makes sense for שאלה to be the deciding moment, because that is when the borrower brings the animal into his domain.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that the borrowing is more important, because that is when he brings the animal into his domain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the time of borrowing, and not the time of loss, is the moment that counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower's responsibility starts when the animal comes into his possession, at the time of שאלה. So that is the moment that defines the borrowing, and the owner's presence then decides whether this counts as שאלה בבעלים.

keyTerms.meaning: it is reasonable / it makes sense

steps.whatToRemember: This is the first reason offered for making שאלה the key moment. The next steps push back on it, and step 9 gives the reason that finally holds: the borrower must feed the animal from the moment of borrowing.

phrases.english: It is reasonable that the borrowing is weightier,
because with it he brings the animal into his domain.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִסְתַּבְּרָא שְׁאֵלָה עֲדִיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reasoning: one moment is more important than the other.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The split could go either way.
steps.terutzMaskana: The time of borrowing is chosen because it brings the animal into the borrower's domain.

steps.title: Pushback: the moment of injury or death should matter more
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues the opposite of step 5: the time of שבורה ומתה should be the deciding moment, since that is when the borrower becomes liable for accidents.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! The time when the animal is injured or dies is more important, because that is when the borrower becomes liable for accidents.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from step 5. It says the moment of injury or death seems more important than the moment of borrowing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 said שאלה is key because that is when the animal enters the borrower's domain. This step points out that the actual obligation to pay only begins when the accident happens. So maybe that moment should decide whether the owner's presence exempts him.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary (introduces the opposite argument)
Is more important / carries more weight
Injured or dead (the moment of the damage)

phrases.english: On the contrary,
the time of injury or death is more important,
since that is when he becomes liable for accidents!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּרַבָּה, שְׁבוּרָה וּמֵתָה עֲדִיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 5's reason for choosing שאלה as the deciding moment.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 5's claim that שאלה is the deciding moment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Liability for אונסין only comes into being at the moment of injury or death, so that moment seems more central.

steps.title: Without the borrowing, the injury means nothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defends שאלה: if there had been no borrowing, the injury or death would create no liability at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: If not for the borrowing, what would the injury or death accomplish?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers back for שאלה. The injury only creates liability because a borrowing happened first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The injury cannot make anyone liable on its own. The borrowing is the foundation that makes the injury count, so the borrowing should be the more important moment.

keyTerms.meaning: What does it accomplish / what effect does it have?

phrases.english: If there were no borrowing,
what would the injury or death accomplish?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי לָא שְׁאֵלָה, שְׁבוּרָה וּמֵתָה מַאי עָבֵיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 6 by showing the injury depends on the borrowing.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing which event the other one depends on
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The injury matters more because the debt begins then.
steps.terutzMaskana: The injury only matters because of the earlier borrowing.

steps.title: But without the injury, the borrowing means nothing either
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the argument around: without injury or death, the borrowing would never make the borrower pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if there were no injury or death, what would the borrowing accomplish?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that step 7's argument works in both directions. Without an injury, the borrowing alone never makes him pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each event needs the other to create liability, so 'one depends on the other' does not settle the question. The two moments are now tied again, and the גמרא needs a new reason to prefer one.

keyTerms.meaning: If not for / were it not for

phrases.english: But if there were no injury or death,
what would the borrowing accomplish?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי לָאו שְׁבוּרָה וּמֵתָה, שְׁאֵלָה מַאי עָבֵיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reverses step 7's logic to cancel it out.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 7's argument that the injury depends on the borrowing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same dependence runs both ways, so it cannot prove that שאלה is more important.

steps.title: The borrowing still wins: the borrower must feed the animal
steps.stepSummary: Even so, שאלה is more important, because from the moment of borrowing the borrower is obligated to feed the animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even so, the borrowing is more important, since from then on he is responsible for the animal's food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new reason that settles the debate in favor of שאלה. The borrowing creates a real, immediate duty: feeding the animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The injury creates an obligation only if an accident happens. The borrowing creates an actual duty right away, because the borrower must feed the animal. That makes the borrowing the stronger starting point, so the owner's presence is checked at the time of שאלה.
steps.whatToRemember: The reasoning ends with שאלה as the key moment. From the time of borrowing the borrower already carries a real duty, feeding the animal.

phrases.english: Even so, the borrowing is more important,
since he is obligated in its food.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲפִילּוּ הָכִי שְׁאֵלָה עֲדִיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Breaks the tie from step 8 with a new reason.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both moments seem equal, since each needs the other.
steps.terutzMaskana: שאלה wins, because the borrower's duty to feed the animal starts then.

steps.title: רב אשי proves it from the words of the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reads 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ' to mean the owner was not with the borrower when he borrowed. Only then does the borrower pay; if the owner was with him, he is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The verse says, 'And if a man borrows from with his fellow.' This means his fellow was not with him, and then 'he shall surely pay.' But if his fellow was with him, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a different proof that the time of borrowing is what counts. He finds it in the opening words of the borrowing פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ' describe the borrowing itself. רב אשי reads them as telling us the owner was not 'with' the borrower at that moment. Since this phrase sits right at the borrowing, the deciding time is the שאלה, which matches steps 3 and 9.

phrases.english: רב אשי said,
the verse says:
"And if a man borrows from with his fellow" —
phrases.notes: שמות 22:13. He reads 'מֵעִם' as 'away from being with': the owner was not with him.

phrases.english: and his fellow was not with him —
"he shall surely pay";
but if his fellow was with him, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר, אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a proof from the פסוק in place of the reasoning in steps 5-9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whether the owner was present is judged at the time of borrowing, as shown by 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ'.

steps.title: Then why does the Torah need the later phrases?
steps.stepSummary: If 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ' already teaches the rule, the phrases 'בְּעָלָיו אֵין עִמּוֹ' and 'אִם בְּעָלָיו עִמּוֹ' seem to be extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why do I need 'its owner is not with him' and 'if its owner is with him'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אשי. If the opening words already teach the law, the Torah's later phrases about the owner seem unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah does not repeat itself for no reason. If רב אשי's reading is right, the later phrases teach nothing new. That suggests the opening words may not have been meant as a lesson at all.

phrases.english: If so,
"its owner is not with him"
and "if its owner is with him" — why do I need them?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי: ״בְּעָלָיו אֵין עִמּוֹ״, וְ״אִם בְּעָלָיו עִמּוֹ״ לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אשי's proof from the פסוק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: His reading makes the later phrases about the owner extra, and the Torah has no extra words.

steps.title: The later phrases show that 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ' is a real lesson
steps.stepSummary: Without the later phrases, we would have thought 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ' was just ordinary wording. The later phrases show the owner's presence matters, so the opening words can be read as a lesson.
steps.simpleTranslation: If not for those phrases, I would have said that this is just the verse's normal way of speaking.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The later phrases are needed so that we take 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ' seriously as a lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On its own, 'borrows from his fellow' sounds like a normal way to describe borrowing. The later phrases show that the owner being 'with him' changes the law. That signals the opening words are also carrying a lesson, and they point to the time of borrowing.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse's normal way of speaking

steps.whatToRemember: רב אשי: 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ' places the deciding moment at the borrowing. The later phrases about the owner are needed so we know to read those opening words as a lesson.
steps.confusionAlert: The later phrases are not extra. They teach that the owner's presence matters, and that is why we may read 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ' as a lesson about when it matters.

phrases.english: If not for those,
I would have said:
this is just the verse's normal way of speaking.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי לָאו הָנָךְ, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 11 and keeps רב אשי's proof standing.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining why the later words are needed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ' is just normal wording with no lesson.
steps.terutzMaskana: The later phrases show the owner's presence matters, so 'מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ' teaches that the time of borrowing decides.

steps.title: Borrowing an animal for a forbidden, unusual purpose
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא asks whether someone who borrowed an animal for a sinful use (bestiality) counts as a שואל. Does a שואל need to borrow the way people normally borrow, or is any benefit enough?
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא asked: if someone borrowed an animal in order to sin with it, what is the law? Do we need borrowing the way people normally borrow, and people don't normally borrow for this? Or perhaps the reason a borrower pays is that he gets benefit, and this person also gets benefit?
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא opens a new question. Is a person who borrowed an animal for a sinful, unusual use treated as a regular שואל, who pays even for accidents?
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to understand why a שואל is so responsible. Maybe the Torah only means normal borrowing, and nobody normally borrows for this. Or maybe the key is simply that the borrower gets הנאה (benefit), and this man did get benefit, even though it was a forbidden one.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked. This introduces a real question (a בעיא) that the גמרא wants to settle.
To commit bestiality with it, a severe sin.
Or perhaps. This introduces the second side of the question.
Benefit or enjoyment the borrower gets from the item

steps.confusionAlert: This is not asking whether the act is allowed. It is clearly a sin. The only question is about money: if the animal dies or is hurt, does this borrower have to pay like a שואל?

phrases.english: Rami bar Chama asked:
If he borrowed it in order to commit bestiality with it, what is the law?
Do we require borrowing the way people normally borrow,
and people do not borrow for this purpose?

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא טַעְמָא מַאי – מִשּׁוּם הֲנָאָה
phrases.english: Or perhaps, what is the reason a borrower pays? Because of the benefit he gets,

phrases.aramaic: וְהַאי נָמֵי הָא אִית לֵיהּ הֲנָאָה
phrases.english: and this person also has benefit.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new set of questions about what counts as borrowing. It moves away from the פסוק reading of מֵעִם רֵעֵהוּ.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a שואל's full responsibility based on normal borrowing, or on any benefit at all, even a forbidden and unusual one?

steps.title: Borrowing only to be seen with the item
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא asks about someone who borrowed an item just to be seen with it, so people think he is rich. Is an item with money value enough, or must he get real use out of it?
steps.simpleTranslation: If he borrowed it just to be seen with it, what is the law? Do we only need something with money value, and that is here? Or perhaps we need something with money value that he gets real benefit from, and that is missing?
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא asks a second question. What if the borrower never uses the item and only shows it off?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the item itself is clearly worth money. The question is whether that is enough, or whether the borrower must also get real, practical use from it. Looking rich is not the kind of use the item was made for.

keyTerms.meaning: To be seen with it, meaning to show off
It is here / it is not here

phrases.english: If he borrowed it to be seen with it, what is the law?
phrases.notes: He means he only wants people to see him with it so they think he is wealthy.

phrases.english: Do we require something of money value, and that is here?
Or perhaps something of money value that he has
benefit from is what we require, and that is not here?

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁאָלָהּ לֵירָאוֹת בָּהּ, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second question from the same series. It moves from forbidden benefit to benefit with no practical use.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is borrowing an item of money value enough to make him a שואל, or must he also get real use from it?

steps.title: Borrowing for use worth less than a פרוטה
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא asks about borrowing to do work worth less than a פרוטה. Does a tiny amount still count as money, or is anything under a פרוטה treated as nothing?
steps.simpleTranslation: If he borrowed it to do work worth less than a פרוטה, what is the law? Do we need money value, and there is some here? Or perhaps anything less than a פרוטה counts as nothing?
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא asks a third question. What if the borrower's use is worth only a tiny amount?
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is real money value here, but very little. In many places in the law, less than a פרוטה is treated as worth nothing. The question is whether that rule applies here too, so that this person would not count as a שואל.

keyTerms.meaning: The smallest coin that counts in the law
It is nothing, meaning it counts as zero

phrases.english: If he borrowed it to do work with it
worth less than a פרוטה, what is the law?
Do we require money value, and there is some here?
Or perhaps anything less than a פרוטה
is nothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁאָלָהּ לַעֲשׂוֹת בָּהּ פָּחוֹת מִפְּרוּטָה, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third question from the same series. Now there is real use, but the amount is tiny.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does benefit worth less than a פרוטה count as money value, enough to make him a שואל?

steps.title: Two cows whose work together is worth one פרוטה
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא asks about borrowing two cows whose work adds up to one פרוטה. Do we count the total between borrower and lender, or each cow on its own?
steps.simpleTranslation: If he borrowed two cows to do work worth a פרוטה, what is the law? Do we say: look at the borrower and lender, and there is a פרוטה? Or perhaps look at the cows, and each one alone has no money value?
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא asks a fourth question, building on the last one. Here the total use is a full פרוטה, but each cow gives only half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we look at the deal between the two people, the borrower got a whole פרוטה of benefit from the lender. If we look at each cow separately, each one gave less than a פרוטה. That would be 'nothing' if the side from Step 15 that says anything under a פרוטה counts as nothing is correct.

keyTerms.meaning: Go after, meaning judge by this

steps.whatToRemember: All four questions test one idea: what makes someone a שואל? Is it normal borrowing, any benefit, real useful benefit, or benefit worth at least a פרוטה, and how is that measured? The גמרא does not answer any of them here.

phrases.english: If he borrowed two cows
to do work with them worth a פרוטה in total, what is the law?
Do we say: go after
the borrower and lender, and there is a פרוטה here?
Or perhaps: go after the cows,
and each one alone does not have money value?
phrases.notes: Each cow did only half a פרוטה's worth of work, less than the smallest amount that counts.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאַל שְׁתֵּי פָּרוֹת לַעֲשׂוֹת בָּהֶן פְּרוּטָה, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the פרוטה question: if less than a פרוטה counts as nothing, how do we measure when there are two animals?
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the פרוטה measured by the whole deal between borrower and lender, or by each animal separately?

steps.title: Borrowing from two partners when only one partner works for the borrower
steps.stepSummary: Someone borrows an animal owned by two partners, and only one of the partners works for him. Is the borrower exempt?
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone borrowed from partners, and one of them was also working for him, what is the law? Do we need all of the owners to be working for him, which is not the case here? Or perhaps he is at least exempt for the half that belongs to the partner who is working for him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question about the 'owner with him' exemption. Here the animal has two owners, but only one of them is working for the borrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption normally applies when 'its owner' is working for the borrower. The question is whether 'its owner' means every owner, so the borrower gets no exemption at all, or whether the rule can be split, exempting him for the half owned by the working partner.

phrases.english: He borrowed from partners
and one of them was borrowed by him to work for him, what is the law?
Do we require all of its owners
phrases.notes: He means: all the owners must be working for the borrower for the exemption to apply.

phrases.english: and that is missing here?
Or perhaps, from that half which is his
he is at least exempt?

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאַל מִשּׁוּתָּפִין וְנִשְׁאַל לוֹ אֶחָד מֵהֶן, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from questions about what counts as borrowing (steps 13-16) to a new set of questions about the 'owner with him' exemption: who has to be working for the borrower.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does 'its owner' require every owner to be working for the borrower, or can the exemption apply to the half owned by the partner who is working?

steps.title: Two partners borrow, and the owner works for only one of them
steps.stepSummary: Now the partners are on the borrowing side. Two partners borrow an animal, and the owner works for only one of them. Is the exemption still in effect?
steps.simpleTranslation: If partners borrowed, and the owner was borrowed to work for one of them, what is the law? Do we need the owner to work for the whole borrowing side, which is not the case here? Or perhaps he is at least exempt for the half that was borrowed by the partner the owner worked for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא flips the last case. This time there are two borrowers, and the owner works for just one of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 17 the question was about the owners. Here it is about the borrowers. Either the exemption needs the owner to be working for every borrower, or at least the half borrowed by the partner the owner worked for is exempt.

phrases.english: Partners who borrowed
and the owner was borrowed to work for one of them, what is the law?
Do we require the entire borrower, and that is missing?
phrases.notes: He means the owner must work for the whole borrowing side, meaning both partners.

phrases.english: Or perhaps, for that half which he borrowed
he is at least exempt?

steps.triggerLanguage: שׁוּתָּפִין שֶׁשָּׁאֲלוּ וְנִשְׁאַל לְאֶחָד מֵהֶן, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The mirror image of step 17: partners on the borrower's side instead of the lender's side.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Must the owner work for all the borrowers, or is the half borrowed by the partner he worked for exempt?

steps.title: Husband and wife: does owning the profits count as owning the thing?
steps.stepSummary: Two cases: someone borrows from a woman and her husband works for him, or a woman borrows and the owner works for her husband. Both depend on whether קנין פירות is like קנין הגוף.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone borrowed from a woman and her husband was borrowed to work for him, or a woman borrowed and the owner was borrowed to work for her husband, what is the law? Is ownership of the profits like ownership of the thing itself, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks two husband-and-wife cases together. It points out that both come down to one question: does a husband's right to use his wife's property make him count as an owner?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A husband has the right to use his wife's property and its profits (קנין פירות), but she owns the item itself (קנין הגוף). If profit-ownership counts like full ownership, the husband counts as the 'owner' in the first case. In the second case he would count as the borrower's side, so the exemption would apply. If it does not count, it would not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: Ownership of the use and profits of something

steps.whyThisMatters: The question of whether קנין פירות is like קנין הגוף comes up all over ש״ס. Here it decides who counts as 'the owner' for the exemption.

phrases.english: If he borrowed from a woman and her husband was borrowed to work for him,
or a woman borrowed and the owner was borrowed to work for the husband, what is the law?
Is ownership of the profits like ownership of the thing itself,
or not?

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאַל מֵהָאִשָּׁה וְנִשְׁאַל בַּעְלָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After two partner cases, the גמרא moves to a husband and wife, where the husband's ownership is only partial in a different way.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a husband's ownership of the profits (קנין פירות) count like full ownership (קנין הגוף), making him count as owner or borrower for this exemption?

steps.title: Does an owner's agent working for the borrower count as the owner?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רב אשי about an owner who sends his agent to work for the borrower along with his cow. Do we need the actual owner, or does the agent count as him?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: If someone tells his agent, 'Go and work for someone on my behalf, together with my cow,' what is the law? Do we need the actual owner, which is not the case here? Or perhaps a person's agent is like himself, so the owner is there?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא brings a new question to רב אשי. The owner does not work for the borrower himself. He sends his agent to work in his place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'its owner' (בעליו) is with it. If that means the real owner in person, the agent does not help. But the rule שלוחו של אדם כמותו says an agent stands in for the person who sent him, so maybe the agent's work counts as the owner's.

keyTerms.meaning: Be borrowed, meaning go work for someone
A person's agent is like the person himself

steps.whatToRemember: All these questions test one idea: who exactly has to be 'with' the borrower for the exemption to apply. The cases are partners on either side, a husband with profit-rights, and an agent sent by the owner.

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
One who says to his agent

phrases.aramaic: צֵא וְהִשָּׁאֵל לִי עִם פָּרָתִי, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: 'Go and be borrowed for me together with my cow,' what is the law?
Do we require 'its owner' literally, and that is missing,
phrases.notes: The quoted word is from the פסוק, שמות 22:14.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא שְׁלוּחוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם כְּמוֹתוֹ, וְאִיכָּא?
phrases.english: or perhaps a person's agent is like himself, and so the owner is there?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי הָאוֹמֵר לִשְׁלוּחוֹ צֵא וְהִשָּׁאֵל לִי עִם פָּרָתִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new questioner (רבינא) adds another case to the series: the owner is 'present' only through an agent.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the exemption require the actual owner in person, or does שלוחו של אדם כמותו let the agent count as the owner?

steps.title: These questions depend on older disputes
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרב אויא tells רב אשי that the husband question matches the מחלוקת of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש, and the agent question matches the מחלוקת of רבי יונתן and רבי יאשיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא son of רב אויא said to רב אשי: The husband question is the argument of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש. The agent question is the argument of רבי יונתן and רבי יאשיה.
steps.whatsHappening: Someone answers the last two questions by saying they are really older arguments. The גמרא will now show each of those arguments, one at a time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not decide the הלכה. He shows that each question rests on a principle that is already argued about. If you know which side you hold in the older argument, you know the answer to the borrowing question.

keyTerms.meaning: A dispute or argument between חכמים
Agent, someone acting on another's behalf

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha son of Rav Avya said to Rav Ashi:

phrases.aramaic: בַּעַל – פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ,
phrases.english: The husband case is the dispute of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish,
phrases.notes: This is the question from step 19, about a woman's husband working along with the animal.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁלִיחַ – פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן וְרַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה.
phrases.english: the agent case is the dispute of Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya.
phrases.notes: This is רבינא's question from step 20, about the owner sending an agent.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the questions of steps 19 and 20 by linking them to known disputes.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The answers depend on two older disputes: קנין פירות (husband) and שליחות (agent).

steps.title: Selling a field only for its fruits
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the source for the husband dispute. Someone sells a field for its fruits only. רבי יוחנן says the buyer brings ביכורים and recites the declaration. ריש לקיש says he brings but does not recite.
steps.simpleTranslation: The husband case is the argument of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש, as it was said: If someone sells his field to another for its fruits, רבי יוחנן says the buyer brings ביכורים and recites. ריש לקיש says he brings but does not recite.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now shows the first older argument, the one about the husband.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer owns the fruits, not the land itself. The declaration over ביכורים speaks about 'the land You gave me.' So the question is whether the buyer can call the land his.

keyTerms.meaning: For its fruits only, not the land itself
Brings ביכורים and recites the declaration

phrases.aramaic: בַּעַל – פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ.
phrases.english: The husband case is the dispute of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.
As it was stated:
One who sells his field to his fellow for its fruits,
Rabbi Yochanan says: he brings and recites,
phrases.notes: He brings ביכורים to the Temple and says the declaration from דברים 26.

phrases.aramaic: רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אוֹמֵר: מֵבִיא וְאֵינוֹ קוֹרֵא,
phrases.english: Reish Lakish says: he brings but does not recite.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּעַל – פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ. דְּאִיתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the first dispute mentioned in step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A buyer of a field's fruits brings ביכורים. רבי יוחנן says he also recites; ריש לקיש says he does not.

steps.title: Is owning the fruits like owning the field?
steps.stepSummary: The reason for the dispute: רבי יוחנן holds that קנין פירות is like קנין הגוף, and ריש לקיש holds it is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says he brings and recites, because owning the fruits is like owning the thing itself. ריש לקיש says he brings but does not recite, because owning the fruits is not like owning the thing itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reason behind each side, and this is the key to the husband question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A husband has rights to the fruits of his wife's property, a קנין פירות. According to רבי יוחנן he counts as an owner, so his working could count as the owner working. According to ריש לקיש he does not count as the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Owning only the right to use a thing and its produce

steps.whatToRemember: The husband case depends on whether קנין פירות counts as קנין הגוף: yes for רבי יוחנן, no for ריש לקיש.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan says he brings and recites:
ownership of the fruits is like ownership of the thing itself.

phrases.aramaic: וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אוֹמֵר מֵבִיא וְאֵינוֹ קוֹרֵא:
phrases.english: And Reish Lakish says he brings but does not recite:

phrases.aramaic: קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת לָאו כְּקִנְיַן הַגּוּף דָּמֵי.
phrases.english: ownership of the fruits is not like ownership of the thing itself.

steps.triggerLanguage: קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת כְּקִנְיַן הַגּוּף דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind the dispute quoted in step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן: קנין פירות is like קנין הגוף. ריש לקיש: it is not.

steps.title: A steward cancels a wife's vows: רבי יאשיה
steps.stepSummary: The source for the agent dispute: a husband appoints a steward to cancel his wife's vows. רבי יאשיה says the cancellation does not work, because the פסוק says only 'her husband' can cancel.
steps.simpleTranslation: The agent case is the argument of רבי יונתן and רבי יאשיה, as taught in a ברייתא: A man tells his steward, 'Any vows my wife makes from now until I return from such a place, cancel them for her,' and the steward cancelled them. You might think they are cancelled. So the פסוק says, 'Her husband confirms it and her husband cancels it.' These are the words of רבי יאשיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now shows the second older argument, about the agent. Here it gives רבי יאשיה's side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יאשיה reads 'her husband' as meaning only the husband himself, so an agent cannot stand in for him here. In the borrowing case, that would mean the owner's agent does not count as the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Steward or manager of a household

phrases.aramaic: שָׁלִיחַ – פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן וְרַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה.
phrases.english: The agent case is the dispute of Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya.
As it is taught:
One who says to a steward:
All vows that my wife will vow
from now until I come back from such-and-such a place,
cancel them for her, and he cancelled them for her,
one might think they would be cancelled,
the verse says: "Her husband confirms it and her husband cancels it,"
these are the words of Rabbi Yoshiya.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁלִיחַ – פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן וְרַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה. דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the second dispute mentioned in step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יאשיה: a steward cannot cancel the wife's vows; only the husband himself can.

steps.title: רבי יונתן: a person's agent is like himself
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן disagrees: everywhere in הלכה, a person's שליח counts as the person himself, so the steward's cancellation works.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונתן says: We find everywhere that a person's agent is like himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the other side of the agent argument. That finishes showing both disputes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יונתן, the general rule of שליחות wins over the wording 'her husband.' Applied to the borrowing case, the owner's agent would count as the owner working. For רבי יאשיה, he would not count.

keyTerms.meaning: A person's agent is like himself

steps.whatToRemember: The agent case depends on whether שלוחו של אדם כמותו applies here: yes for רבי יונתן, no for רבי יאשיה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yonatan says:

phrases.aramaic: מָצִינוּ בְּכׇל מָקוֹם שֶׁשְּׁלוּחוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם כְּמוֹתוֹ.
phrases.english: We have found everywhere that a person's agent is like himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָצִינוּ בְּכׇל מָקוֹם שֶׁשְּׁלוּחוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם כְּמוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to רבי יאשיה in step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יונתן: a person's agent is like himself, so the steward's cancellation works.

steps.title: רב עיליש asks about lending a slave together with a cow
steps.stepSummary: רב עילישׁ asks רבא what the law is when an owner tells his slave to go and be lent out along with his cow. He adds that the question applies to both opinions about whether a שליח is like the person himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עיליש said to רבא: If someone tells his slave, 'Go and be lent out together with my cow,' what is the law? The question works for the one who says a person's agent is like himself, and it also works for the one who says a person's agent is not like himself.
steps.whatsHappening: A new question is asked: if the owner sends his slave along with the borrowed cow, does that count as the owner himself being lent with it? The גמרא says this question works on both sides of the שליח debate, and the next step explains how.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We just saw the debate between רבי יאשיה and רבי יונתן about whether a שליח counts as the person himself. רב עילישׁ points out that a slave is a different kind of case. So the answer is not automatic under either opinion, and that is why the question is worth asking.

keyTerms.meaning: A slave (here a Canaanite slave owned by his master)
And be lent out (go work for the borrower)
Let the question be asked (the question works according to this opinion)
A person's agent is like himself

phrases.english: Rav Ilish said to Rava:
One who says to his slave:
Go and be lent out together with my cow,
phrases.notes: The slave goes to work for the borrower at the same time the cow is lent. The question is whether that counts as the owner being 'with' his animal.

phrases.english: what is the law?
The question can be asked according to the one who says
a person's agent is like himself,
phrases.notes: This is רבי יונתן's view from the previous step.

phrases.english: and it can be asked according to the one who says
a person's agent is not like himself.
phrases.notes: This is רבי יאשיה's view, the one who said the steward cannot cancel the vows.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב עִילִישׁ לְרָבָא: הָאוֹמֵר לְעַבְדּוֹ צֵא וְהִשָּׁאֵל עִם פָּרָתִי, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the agent debate (steps 24-25) and applies it to a new case: a slave instead of an agent.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does lending one's slave along with one's cow count as the owner himself being lent with it?

steps.title: Why the slave question works on both sides
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the two sides of the question. Even if a שליח counts as the person, maybe a slave doesn't, because he is not fully obligated in מצוות. Even if a שליח does not count, maybe a slave does, because a slave's hand is like his master's hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: It can be asked according to the one who says a person's agent is like himself: maybe that applies only to an agent, who is obligated in מצוות, but a slave, who is not fully obligated in מצוות, does not count. Or perhaps, even according to the one who says a person's agent is not like himself, that applies only to an agent. But a slave is different, because a slave's hand is like his master's hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the 'it can be asked' line to spell out why each opinion still leaves the slave case unclear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: a שליח can stand in for his sender because, like the sender, he is obligated in מצוות. A slave is not fully obligated, so maybe he cannot stand in. Side two: a slave belongs to his master, so 'יד עבד כיד רבו' might make him count as the master even where a regular שליח would not.

keyTerms.meaning: These words apply (only) to... (limits a rule to a certain case)
Or perhaps (introduces the other side of a question)
A slave's hand is like his master's hand. What the slave holds or does belongs to the master.

steps.confusionAlert: The two sides point in opposite directions. The first side says that even under the lenient view of שליחות, a slave might NOT count. The second side says that even under the strict view, a slave MIGHT count. That is why the question works for both opinions.

phrases.english: It can be asked according to the one who says
a person's agent is like himself:
maybe that applies to an agent,
because he is obligated in מצוות.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל עֶבֶד, דְּלָאו בַּר מִצְוָה – לָא.
phrases.english: But a slave, who is not fully obligated in מצוות, does not count.
Or perhaps, even

phrases.aramaic: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר אֵין שְׁלוּחוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם כְּמוֹתוֹ,
phrases.english: according to the one who says a person's agent is not like himself,
that applies only to an agent.
But a slave is different:
a slave's hand is like his master's hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּיבְּעֵי לְמַאן דְּאָמַר שְׁלוּחוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם כְּמוֹתוֹ, הָנֵי מִילֵּי שָׁלִיחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the two-sided framing that step 26 only mentioned.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a slave weaker than a שליח (not obligated in מצוות) or stronger than a שליח (his hand is his master's hand)?

steps.title: רבא answers: a slave's hand is like his master's hand
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that it makes sense to say a slave's hand is like his master's hand. So lending the slave with the cow counts as the owner being with his animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: It makes sense that a slave's hand is like his master's hand.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא picks the second side of the question. The slave counts as his master.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the slave is like an extension of the master, sending him with the cow counts as if the owner himself went along. So the borrower would get the exemption for borrowing with the owner, even according to the view that a regular שליח does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense / it stands to reason
Is similar to / is considered like

steps.whatToRemember: A slave is not just a שליח. Because יד עבד כיד רבו, a slave lent along with the cow counts as the owner being with his animal.

phrases.english: He said to him: It makes sense
that a slave's hand is like his master's hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מִסְתַּבְּרָא יַד עֶבֶד כְּיַד רַבּוֹ דָּמְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question posed in steps 26-27 by choosing the second side.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A slave's hand is like his master's hand, so the slave counts as the owner being with the animal.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא begins a question about a husband and his wife's property
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא opens a new question about a husband and the property of his wife. The rest of the question continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא asked: A husband with regard to his wife's property...
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins here. The גמרא is setting up the next move, and the full question comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the property the husband may use and eat the profits from during the marriage, but which goes back to his wife if the marriage ends. רמי בר חמא is about to ask how the husband is treated with regard to this property.

phrases.english: Rami bar Chama asked:
A husband with regard to his wife's property...

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא: בַּעַל בְּנִכְסֵי אִשְׁתּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question after the slave question has been answered.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How is a husband treated with regard to his wife's property? The full question continues on the next amud.
